newsitem.title: USA: FDA asks judge to permit tobacco regulation.
newsitem.headline: FDA asks judge to permit tobacco regulation.

text.p: The Food and Drug Administration Monday asked a federal court here to turn down a tobacco industry request that tough new tobacco regulations be blocked.
The Clinton adminstration stunned the tobacco industry in August by giving the FDA extensive new regulatory powers over the sale and marketing of cigarettes in a bid to curb smoking among children.
The agency said in a court filing that its sharp restrictions on tobacco billboards, vending machines and sports advertisements were consistent with the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act.
"By enacting the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, Congress provided the Food and Drug Adminstration with the authority to regulate cigarettes and smokeless tobacco ...," the FDA said.
The regulations ban billboards within 1,000 feet of schools and playgrounds and all cigarette vending machines except for those in nightclubs and other places where minors are barred.
The rules also end distribution of free samples of cigarettes, brand-name sponsorship of sporting events and the placement of cigarette names on hats, tee-shirts, gym bags and other products.
Such promotion has been key to the tobacco industry in the decades since industry advertising was removed from U.S. television broadcasts.

Cigarette makers and advertisers struck back on Oct. 15 by filing a motion in the U.S. District Court for central North Carolina for a summary judgment against the FDA. They argued that the agency does not have jurisdiction to regulate tobacco products.

The motion claimed Congress never authorised the FDA to regulate cigarettes and smokeless tobacco; that the act did not authorise the FDA to regulate those products as "drugs" or medical devices; and that the restrictions on advertising violated free-speech guarantees.

"If FDA's assertion of juridiction is sustained, there can be no reasonable doubt that FDA can do everything it can to stamp out tobacco in the United States ...," the tobacco companies and advertising agencies said in their filing.
The plaintiffs include Philip Morris Cos. Inc., the Brown & Williamson unit of B.A.T Industries, RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.'s RJ Reynolds Tobacco Co., and Loews Corp.'s Lorillard Tobacco Inc.

Coyne Beam Inc. and other advertising agencies and trade groups are also plaintiffs, seeking to stop regulations that would limit advertising in youth-oriented publications to black-and-white text only.
The FDA said in Monday's filing that "restrictions adopted by FDA on advertising and other promotional activities for cigarettes are consistent with the First Amendment."
